newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Yeltsin foes tighten pressure with local poll wins.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin foes tighten pressure with local poll wins.

text.p: Russian nationalists and communists celebrated big victories on Monday in three local elections, serving President Boris Yeltsin notice of deep discontent with the Kremlin before a day of strikes.

In a sign of the disillusionment over unpaid wages and pensions Vasily Starodubtsev, one of the leaders of a hardline coup against Soviet President Mikhail Gorbachev in 1991, was among the winners in Sunday's three local polls.

Yeltsin has promised to end the wage delays and promoted young liberal reformers to do so in a still incomplete government reshuffle. But he has failed to head off a day of nationwide protests planned by trade unions for Thursday.

"Our schools, science are rotting away. In two or three years' time we will have become like some second-rate African country," former Soviet dissident Alexander Solzhenitsyn told NTV commercial television on Sunday evening.
"There is a terrifying split in society...We are in great danger now," said the Nobel laureate who is now a critic of the new capitalist Russia.

The government has signalled its concern over social tensions by beefing up security arrangements for Thursday's protests, which the organisers say will involve millions of people in strikes and protest rallies.

Yeltsin, 66, was resting on Monday after last week's summit with U.S. President Bill Clinton in Helsinki. But he was due to finish his cabinet reshuffle and receive India's visiting prime minister before Thursday's strikes.

Regional elections are often a way for voters to let off steam against the government. The Kremlin is likely to play down the significance of Sunday's results, especially as Yeltsin has clearly reasserted his grip on power after illness.

But the outcome was a reminder of Yeltsin's pressing need to show the Russian people that reforms are under way again after what many regard as a period of stagnation since he went down with heart problems last summer.
Communist-backed candidates won two of Sunday's elections and a nationalist won the third.
Itar-Tass news agency said communist-backed Starodubtsev won 60 percent of the votes in an election for governor of Tula, south of Moscow, and secured a seat in parliament's upper house.
Starodubtsev was a member of the eight-men committee of hardliners who tried to overthrow Gorbachev in 1991 and failed because of defiance led by Yeltsin.

Communist Anatoly Belonogov scored a similarly easy victory for the governorship of the Amur region bordering China, and nationalist Dmitry Rogozin won a seat in the lower house of parliament in an election in the southern region of Voronezh.
Rogozin is head of the nationalist Congress of Russian Communities which has cooperated closely with general Alexander Lebed, an outspoken Yeltsin opponent.

Criticism of the government is expected to reach a peak in Thursday's protests, although Yeltsin has already made major changes by bringing young reformers Anatoly Chubais and Boris Nemtsov into the cabinet to take over the economic reforms.
Yeltsin will briefly turn his attention away from economic problems and his reshuffle to meet Indian Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda on Tuesday.

He is also expected to meet Chinese Foreign Minister Qian Qichen this week in talks turning Russian eyes east at a time of strains with the West over NATO's plans to take in new members from the former Soviet bloc. Moscow opposes the enlargement.
